title_en: Summary of the National Juvenile Court Work Conference
full_text_en:
Summary of the National Conference on Work of Juvenile Courts of Courts

Fa [1995] No. 112

From May 8 to 12, 1995, the Supreme People's Court held the "National Conference on Work of Juvenile Courts of Courts" in Fujian Province.

Wang Jingrong, Vice President of the Supreme People's Court and Head of the Juvenile Court Steering Group, attended the conference and delivered speeches at the beginning and end of the meeting.

This conference reviewed and summarized the achievements and experience gained in the construction and work of juvenile courts, and studied issues concerning further strengthening the construction of juvenile courts and the adjudication of cases involving minors in the coming period. The participating comrades unanimously agreed that this conference was timely and successful. The summary is as follows.

(I)

The conference reviewed the development process of juvenile court work over the past decade, focusing on a careful summary of juvenile court work nationwide since 1990. In November 1984, the Changning District People's Court of Shanghai established the first juvenile court in China. After trials in various localities, in 1988 the Supreme People's Court held an experience exchange meeting on the trial of criminal cases involving minors in Shanghai, promoting juvenile court work experience nationwide, and juvenile courts rapidly spread across the country. In 1990, the Supreme People's Court held a national conference on juvenile criminal trial work in Nanjing, further promoting the development of juvenile court work. As of the end of 1994, courts nationwide had established 3,369 juvenile courts, including 540 independently established juvenile criminal trial tribunals and 249 comprehensive tribunals handling criminal, civil, and economic cases involving the protection of minors. There were more than 10,000 adjudicators for juvenile cases nationwide.

The conference believed that the "Several Provisions on Handling Juvenile Criminal Cases (Trial)" (hereinafter referred to as the "Provisions") formulated and issued by the Supreme People's Court in January 1991, and the "Notice on Establishing a Mutually Supporting Work System for Handling Juvenile Criminal Cases" and the "Joint Notice on Inviting Special Jurors for the Trial of Juvenile Criminal Cases" jointly issued by the Supreme People's Court with the Supreme People's Procuratorate, the Ministry of Public Security, the Ministry of Justice, the State Education Commission, and organizations such as trade unions, the Communist Youth League, and women's federations in June 1991, standardized the procedures for handling juvenile criminal cases, established the basic principles of juvenile criminal trial activities, promoted the development of work to protect minors, and facilitated the implementation of comprehensive social governance measures. As of the end of 1994, courts nationwide had invited more than 13,000 special jurors from departments and organizations such as trade unions, the Communist Youth League, women's federations, and education departments. They played an active role in participating in the trial of cases and implementing assistance and education measures.

The conference fully affirmed the achievements of juvenile court work. It was believed that over the past ten years, juvenile courts had gone through stages of initiation, piloting, experience promotion, and comprehensive development, and had now entered a stage of consolidation, improvement, and standardized development. According to statistics, from 1984 to the end of 1994, courts nationwide sentenced more than 360,000 juvenile offenders, a considerable portion of whom were tried by juvenile courts, especially in recent years where the vast majority of juvenile offenders were tried and sentenced by juvenile courts. After juvenile offenders sentenced by juvenile courts were educated and reformed and returned to society, they generally were able to reform and make a fresh start, and the recidivism rate decreased significantly. Therefore, the work of juvenile courts received unanimous praise from all sectors of society and the general public, and was also commended by relevant international organizations and friendly individuals.

On the basis of full discussion, the conference unanimously agreed that the main experience in the construction and work of juvenile courts includes the following aspects:

First, Comrade Deng Xiaoping's theory of building socialism with Chinese characteristics and the Party's basic line are the fundamental guiding principles for the construction and work of juvenile courts.

Second, the attention and support of leaders at all levels of courts are important guarantees for doing a good job in juvenile court work.

Third, focusing on the institutional and organizational building of juvenile courts is the foundation for strengthening the trial of cases involving minors.

Fourth, adhering to the principle of "integrating education into adjudication and combining punishment with education" is the main characteristic of juvenile court work and a concrete manifestation of the superiority of China's socialist system. It is also an inheritance and development of the fine tradition of judicial work that combines specialized work with the mass line.

Fifth, establishing a "two-dragon" work system, closely cooperating and coordinating with various political and legal departments and relevant social aspects, is an effective measure to improve the quality of trial work, consolidate court hearing effects, and achieve the purpose of preventing and correcting juvenile delinquency.

Sixth, continuously summarizing experience and strengthening theoretical research are important factors in promoting the construction of juvenile courts and the in-depth development of trial work.

(II)

The conference pointed out that after ten years of exploration and development, although great achievements have been made in juvenile court work and much good experience has been accumulated, the results are still preliminary. As a national judicial system, it still needs to mature and improve. From a national perspective, there are still some deficiencies and problems in current juvenile court work that need to be seriously studied and resolved. For example, understanding of juvenile courts is not entirely consistent, development is unbalanced across regions, and certain work systems and specific practices are not sufficiently uniform and standardized. In accordance with the requirements of the overall national situation for court work, and in light of existing problems, the conference proposed the basic tasks for juvenile court work in the coming period, summarized in twelve characters: consolidate, strengthen, enrich, standardize, improve, and develop.

First, consolidate the achievements already made. Whether in work practice or theoretical research, achievements must be consolidated. In particular, achievements in organizational structures, work systems, and team building need to be further consolidated.

Second, continue to strengthen the construction of juvenile court organizations and work systems. In areas where organizational construction and work have been well developed, complacency and slackness must not be allowed; instead, further efforts should be made to achieve greater results. In areas where work has progressed slowly and the foundation is relatively weak, through this conference, advanced experience should be learned, gaps should be identified, and efforts should be made to catch up. Where juvenile courts should have been established but have not, or where only a signboard has been hung but work has not been effectively carried out in accordance with relevant regulations, organizations and personnel should be put in place as soon as possible, and work should be earnestly initiated.

Third, enrich the work force of juvenile courts. Currently, juvenile delinquency in China is generally on the rise. Preventing and correcting juvenile delinquency will be a long-term important task for political and legal departments. The task of people's courts in adjudicating juvenile criminal cases is heavy. The work force should not only not be weakened but should be enriched and strengthened as much as possible. When existing cadres retire, outstanding adjudicators should be selected to replace them as soon as possible. When selecting personnel, attention should be paid to ensuring an appropriate proportion of female judges as required by the Provisions.

Fourth, standardize the work of juvenile courts. Based on actual conditions, each locality should carefully standardize the structure, staffing, and scope of cases of local juvenile courts. When trying cases involving minors, they should strictly follow the provisions of the Criminal Law, the Criminal Procedure Law, and the relevant judicial interpretations of the Supreme People's Court. Specific practices that have been proven effective through many years of practice should be carefully summarized and, after full research and argumentation, promoted step by step, so that all work of juvenile courts gradually moves onto a standardized and institutionalized track.

Fifth, improve the quality of case handling and the quality of adjudicators. In particular, in places where juvenile court institutions have been established but work has not been fully carried out in accordance with the Supreme People's Court's Provisions, or where the "two-dragon" work system has not been well implemented, greater efforts must be made to take measures to improve work and raise the quality of case handling. To effectively raise the level of adjudication of cases involving minors, training for juvenile court adjudicators must be strengthened to improve their political and professional quality, and especially to cultivate their dedication, sense of responsibility, professionalism, and high professional ethics.

Sixth, continue research and exploration to promote the continuous development and improvement of China's juvenile justice system. China's juvenile courts, as a new thing in reform, have shown vigorous vitality and strong vitality since their birth, but they only have a history of ten years and have just entered their "juvenile period." The future development prospects are broad, and the road ahead is still long. Therefore, we must continue to adhere to the spirit of reform, deeply study and explore, from the combination of theory and practice, how to promote the construction and work of juvenile courts to continuously develop to a new and higher stage.

(III)

Regarding several issues that need to be seriously resolved at present, the participating comrades reached a consensus after full discussion and in-depth study:

First, the issue of the organizational form of juvenile courts. From trial practice, independently established tribunals generally have stronger forces and better working conditions than collegial panels, which is conducive to strengthening the trial of cases involving minors. Currently, each locality should, based on needs and existing conditions, strive to expand on the basis of original collegial panels to establish juvenile criminal trial tribunals. If the number of juvenile criminal cases in the locality is not large and the court's staffing is relatively tight, so that spreading trial forces too thinly would not be conducive to strengthening trial work, the original collegial panel structure may be maintained. In short, decisions should be based on actual conditions, work needs, and existing conditions, without a "one-size-fits-all" approach.

Second, the issue of the scope of cases accepted by juvenile courts. Currently, the scope of cases accepted by juvenile courts in some localities is very inconsistent, which has already affected the internal trial work order of courts and the future development of juvenile courts. The conference believed that juvenile courts should focus on the trial of juvenile criminal cases, and where conditions permit, may undertake the trial of cases involving infringement of the personal rights of minors. The originally piloted "comprehensive tribunals" should carefully summarize experience, weigh the pros and cons, and adjust the scope of cases accepted. In a few localities, in light of actual local conditions, attempts to have juvenile courts accept certain civil cases involving minors as parties may continue piloting, but should not be advocated or promoted on a large scale. Juvenile courts should not accept economic dispute cases.

Third, the issue of applying penalties to juvenile offenders. In handling cases, juvenile courts in all localities must pay attention to adhering to the principle of socialist legality, strictly act in accordance with the law, the Supreme People's Court's judicial interpretations, and normative documents. When sentencing juvenile offenders, they must both adhere to the principle of lighter or mitigated punishment according to law and properly control the extent of lighter or mitigated punishment; they must prevent both the tendency to apply penalties to juvenile offenders without distinction from adult offenders and the tendency to be excessively lenient toward juvenile offenders and impose disproportionately light sentences. They must effectively ensure correct application of the law, with appropriate leniency and severity.

Fourth, the issue of correctly exercising the functions of juvenile courts. As trial organs of the people's courts, the basic function of juvenile courts is to adjudicate cases. Under the premise of centering on trial activities, the people's courts should, in accordance with the requirements of the "Law on the Protection of Minors" and local specific conditions, appropriately extend the work of education, persuasion, and rescue forward, outward, and backward, to fully leverage the advantages and characteristics of the people's courts and actively participate in comprehensive social governance. However, it must be clearly understood that implementing the "Law on the Protection of Minors" is the common responsibility of the whole society. In relevant work, the people's courts should pay attention to correctly positioning themselves, coordinating their relationship with relevant departments, and fully exerting their initiative and proactivity without overstepping their scope of work or replacing other functional departments in exercising their powers.

Fifth, the issue of summarizing one's own experience and drawing on foreign experience. The experience accumulated over ten years of exploration of juvenile courts in China should be further summarized, elevated to the theoretical level, and then used to guide practice, so as to overcome blindness and enhance consciousness. At the same time, we should continue to emancipate our minds and boldly absorb and draw on useful foreign experience. However, learning and using foreign experience must suit China's national conditions, truly achieving "make foreign things serve China," without copying mechanically or divorcing from China's actual situation.

Sixth, the issue of effectively strengthening leadership over juvenile court work. Currently, juvenile court work faces many practical difficulties, and there are also certain instability factors in the cadres team. Therefore, more support and concern need to be given to juvenile courts. The conference emphasized that leading comrades of courts at all levels must fully consider the special nature of juvenile court work when making work arrangements, personnel deployments, selecting outstanding personnel, promotions and rank advancements (including the evaluation of judge ranks), determining post responsibilities, and distributing bonuses and subsidies. They should make correct decisions, treat them fairly, and properly resolve relevant issues to mobilize the enthusiasm of juvenile court staff and create a good environment and conditions for doing better work in the future.

(This publication has been slightly abridged—Editor's note)

July 28, 1995
